title: Hands alone, then together
summary: Split a hard bar into what each hand does, learn each alone, then join them slowly.
materials: the piece from your teacher, with a pencil

figure.alt: A one-octave keyboard from middle C. C4 through G4, five neighbouring keys, are highlighted as one example of a hand position: the shape either hand might rest in while it is learned alone, before the two hands are joined.

steps.title: Hands alone, then together
steps.body:
A hard bar is often two easy bars stacked on top of each other: what the right hand does and what the left hand does. Together they seem impossible. Apart, each one is simple.

1. Take the hard bars. Play the right hand alone, slowly, three times.
2. Play the left hand alone, three times. Say the note names out loud if it helps.
3. Now put them together, very slowly, three times. Stop at the first slip, and go back to the hand that slipped.
4. Finish with the whole piece once through.

Your brain learns one new thing at a time. Splitting the hands gives it one thing at a time, and the joining comes fast once each hand knows its job.

figure.alt: A two-octave keyboard from middle C. The A above middle C and the A one octave higher are highlighted in gold, the two notes the text names: one wiggles 440 times a second, the other 880, exactly twice as fast.

steps.title: Pitch is a wiggle rate
steps.body:
Every note is a wiggle. Press a key and a string inside the piano wiggles back and forth hundreds of times a second, and the air carries that wiggle to your ear. A keyboard has no strings, so it makes the wiggle with electricity instead, but your ear cannot tell.

Faster wiggle, higher note. The A above middle C wiggles 440 times every second. The A one octave higher wiggles 880 times, exactly twice as fast. Go down an octave and it halves to 220.

Predict first: if 440 wiggles a second is the A above middle C, how many for the A two octaves up? Write your number in the Practice log.

Measure: open a free tuner app on the phone, play that A, and read the number it shows. Then play the A two octaves up.

Compare: how close was your prediction? Teach it: tell someone in one sentence why the high keys are on the right.

figure.alt: A one-octave keyboard from middle C, C4 through G4 highlighted as an example hand position, the same shape practised right hand alone, then left hand alone, then together slowly.

steps.title: Four sittings
steps.body: Fifteen minutes each. Tick a sitting when it is done. Days do not matter; sittings do.
checklist: Sitting 1: hard bars, right hand alone three times, left hand alone three times, together three times slowly
Sitting 2: hands alone, then together, then the piece once through
Sitting 3: together only, slowly; stop at the first slip and fix that hand
Sitting 4: the whole piece once through, then again as if recording
An old piece played once, hands together, no stopping

steps.title: Record this week's version
steps.prompt: Say the name of the piece, then play it once through, hands in the frame. Slips stay in.
